A sheep is a medium-sized, four-legged animal that humans have kept and raised for thousands of years. It is one of the most common farm animals in the world. Sheep are covered in a thick, fluffy coat called wool, which humans shear (cut off) to make clothing, blankets, and yarn. Sheep are also raised for their meat and milk.

They have a soft face, hooves, and a tendency to stay close together in groups. Their wool is most commonly white, but can also be black or brown. Some sheep have curved horns (usually males), while others do not.

This is important: the plural of "sheep" is still sheep — not "sheeps." This is one of those unusual English words that does not change in the plural.

  • One sheep was in the field.
  • Twenty sheep were in the field.

More simply put: when a sheep is young, it is called a lamb. Once it grows up, a female is a ewe and a male is a ram.
What a group of sheep is called
A group of sheep is called a flock.

• Wool — their coat, which is sheared once or twice a year and used to make warm clothing
  • Meat — meat from a young sheep is called lamb; meat from an adult sheep is called mutton
  • Milk — used to make certain cheeses (like feta and manchego)

Sheep are known for following each other very closely. If one sheep moves, the others tend to follow. This is because they are herd animals — they feel safe in a group and instinctively stick together. This natural behavior is part of why the word "sheep" is sometimes used to describe people (see below).
The figurative meaning (calling a person a "sheep")

When you call a person a sheep, it is almost always a criticism. It means that person blindly follows what others do or say, without stopping to think for themselves. They go along with the crowd, follow trends without question, or obey authority without using their own judgment.

"He never forms his own opinions — he's such a sheep."

This use comes directly from how actual sheep behave: they follow the herd without question.

These come up often in English, so knowing them is valuable:

1. "A wolf in sheep's clothing"
This describes someone who appears harmless, friendly, or trustworthy on the outside, but is actually dangerous, dishonest, or harmful underneath. The "wolf" (a predator) is hiding inside the "sheep's" (an innocent animal's) appearance.

"Be careful with him — he acts kind, but he's a wolf in sheep's clothing."

2. "The black sheep (of the family)"
In a flock of white sheep, a black sheep stands out as different. So a "black sheep of the family" is a person who is considered odd, embarrassing, or a source of shame compared to the rest of their family or group. It is usually used in a slightly negative or pitying way, though sometimes it is worn as a badge of pride.

"She became a rock musician while everyone else became doctors — the black sheep of the family."

3. "Counting sheep"
This is a popular folk idea for falling asleep: you close your eyes and imagine sheep jumping over a fence, counting each one — one sheep, two sheep, three sheep… The repetition is supposed to bore your mind into sleep. Today it is used as a lighthearted way to talk about trying to fall asleep.

"I was up at 2 AM counting sheep."

4. "Separate the sheep from the goats"
This expression means to sort or divide people (or things) into two clear groups — usually good from bad, capable from incapable, or worthy from unworthy. It comes from the biblical image of a shepherd separating sheep (valued) from goats (less valued).

"The final exam will separate the sheep from the goats."

5. "May as well be hanged for a sheep as for a lamb"
This older expression means: if you are already going to be punished for something small, you might as well go ahead and do the bigger thing too, since the punishment will be the same. It is used to justify doing something bold when you are already in trouble.

"I've already been late once this week — may as well be hanged for a sheep as for a lamb and take the full day off."

A sheep is a woolly farm animal raised for wool, meat, and milk. Its young is a lamb, its female is a ewe, its male is a ram, and a group is a flock. The word never changes in the plural. When used to describe a person, it means someone who follows others without independent thought. And in phrases, it appears in expressions about hidden danger, standing out in a family, trying to sleep, and distinguishing people by their worth.
